hints: Look at the side chain of gingerol and classify the $\text{C-OH}$ group as primary, secondary or tertiary, remembering the phenolic $\text{-OH}$ and $\text{CH}_3\text{O-}$ are unreactive here.
walkthrough:
Spot the oxidisable group**
Look along the gingerol molecule with me. You have a phenol $\text{Ar-OH}$ on the ring, a methoxy $\text{CH}_3\text{O-}$ which you are told is unreactive, a ketone $\text{C=O}$ already present, and one aliphatic $\text{-CH(OH)-}$ in the long chain. Acidified $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ is a strong oxidising agent, but phenols and ketones do not give a clean oxidation to a new functional group under these conditions. The reactive centre is that aliphatic alcohol.

Classify and predict the product**
That $\text{-CH(OH)-}$ carbon is attached to two other carbons, so it is a secondary alcohol. Secondary alcohols are oxidised to ketones, the $\text{-OH}$ is replaced by $\text{C=O}$. So the type is oxidation, from alcohol to ketone (carbonyl).

Final answer: type of reaction: oxidation
functional group change: from secondary alcohol ($\text{-OH}$) to ketone ($\text{C=O}$ / carbonyl)

hints: Compare gingerol and shogaol side by side and identify what small molecule has been lost from the $\text{-CO-CH}_2\text{-CH(OH)-}$ unit to give $\text{-CO-CH=CH-}$.
walkthrough:
Play spot the difference**
Put the two structures together. Gingerol has $\text{-CO-CH}_2\text{-CH(OH)-CH}_2\text{-}$ while shogaol has $\text{-CO-CH=CH-CH}_2\text{-}$ in exactly the same place. The $\text{-OH}$ and a neighbouring $\text{-H}$ have gone, and a $\text{C=C}$ has appeared. Losing $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ from an alcohol to make an alkene is dehydration, which is a type of elimination reaction.
Final answer: dehydration / elimination (of water to form an alkene)

hints: Recall the standard laboratory way to dehydrate an alcohol without oxidising it, think of passing vapour over a hot catalyst or warming with a concentrated acid that removes water.
walkthrough:
Choose dehydration, not oxidation**
You must not use an oxidising acid like nitric acid or dichromate here, you only want to remove water. The classic reagents are heat with $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$, or heat with concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ or concentrated $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$. All act by promoting elimination of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ to give the $\text{C=C}$ in shogaol.

Final answer: reagents: concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ or concentrated $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$ (or $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$)
conditions: heat

hints: Remember hot, concentrated acidified $\text{MnO}_4^-$ cleaves every $\text{C=C}$ completely, each alkene carbon ends up as a $\text{C=O}$ that is further oxidised if it still has H or alkyl attached.
Split shogaol at the $\text{-CO-CH=CH-}$ bond and think what the left $\text{-CO-CH=}$ fragment and the right $\text{=CH-alkyl}$ fragment each become under vigorous oxidation.
walkthrough:
Locate the cleavage point**
Hot, concentrated $\text{MnO}_4^-$/$\text{H}^+$ does not give a diol, it smashes the $\text{C=C}$ apart. In shogaol the only $\text{C=C}$ is $\text{-C(=O)-CH=CH-(CH}_2)_n\text{CH}_3$. Draw a line right through that double bond. You will get two carbonyl fragments.

Work out the left fragment Q**
The left alkene carbon is $\text{-CO-CH=}$. On cleavage it first becomes $\text{-CO-CHO}$, an aldehyde next to a ketone. Under hot concentrated conditions aldehydes are oxidised straight on to carboxylic acids. So $\text{-CO-CHO}$ becomes $\text{-CO-CO}_2\text{H}$. The rest of the molecule, the disubstituted benzene with $\text{HO-}$ and $\text{CH}_3\text{O-}$ and the $\text{-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{-CO-}$ part, is untouched. That gives Q as $\text{HO-C}_6\text{H}_4(\text{OCH}_3)\text{-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{C(=O)CO}_2\text{H}$.

Work out the right fragment R**
The right alkene carbon is $\text{=CH-alkyl}$. Cleavage gives $\text{O=CH-alkyl}$, an aldehyde, which is then oxidised to $\text{HO}_2\text{C-alkyl}$. Counting the alkyl chain in shogaol, this is $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_4\text{CO}_2\text{H}$, hexanoic acid. That is R.

Final answer: Q: $\text{HO-C}_6\text{H}_3(\text{OCH}_3)\text{-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{C(=O)CO}_2\text{H}$, the aromatic ring unchanged with $\text{OH}$ and $\text{OCH}_3$ ortho to each other and side chain $\text{-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{-C(=O)-CO}_2\text{H}$
R: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ (hexanoic acid)

hints: Recall which functional group couples with benzenediazonium chloride in alkaline solution at $5^{\circ}\text{C}$ to give a coloured azo dye precipitate.
Use the pair of carbonyl tests together: 2,4-DNPH tells you if any $\text{C=O}$ is present, while Tollens tells you whether that $\text{C=O}$ is an aldehyde or a ketone.
walkthrough:
Decode the azo coupling result**
Benzenediazonium chloride at $5^{\circ}\text{C}$ in alkali is the classic coupling test. A red or orange precipitate of an azo dye forms only with phenols (or aromatic amines). Zingerone gives a red ppt., so it must contain a phenol group, the $\text{Ar-OH}$ you saw in gingerol and shogaol.

Combine the two carbonyl tests**
2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine gives an orange ppt. with any aldehyde or ketone, so you know a $\text{C=O}$ is present. Warm Tollens reagent gives a silver mirror only with aldehydes, which are easily oxidised. Here there is no change, so no aldehyde is present. Orange with 2,4-DNPH plus negative Tollens can only mean a ketone.

Final answer: benzenediazonium chloride, red ppt. indicates phenol
2,4-DNPH orange ppt. plus no change with Tollens indicates ketone (carbonyl present but not aldehyde)
